source.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how automated-interpretability scores respond to evaluation-data construction and scoring choices, and argues that such scores need explanation-free baselines. It refines the measurement claim, but does not test whether neurons are polysemantic.
record.gate_note: The measured outcomes are automated explanation and simulation scores, not counts or classifications of polysemantic neurons. Rows below bear on V7's measurement component only; the study does not measure polysemanticity itself. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows. The matched-mark construction is derived but not built or scored.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether automated-interpretability scores (fuzzing balanced accuracy, simulation correlation) can be reached by explanation-free rules that read how evaluation items are built. It never classifies any neuron or SAE feature as polysemantic or monosemantic, and never counts how often that happens. Its outcome is the reliability of explanation scores, a related but different construct. So it does not test V7 or any other version. It mentions monosemanticity work only as background citations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that a construction-reading rule beats the stored LLM scorers on every stored fuzzing set they measured. They state that a sequence-order rule beats GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). They recommend random-offset windows with the BOS token, negatives marked from the positives' law, and reporting the within-sequence part of simulation scores.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates explanation and simulation scores under alternate data constructions, explanation-free baselines, and scoring rubrics; it does not reproduce the original neuron polysemanticity measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Scores vary with evaluation-data construction (stored peak-centred snippets versus random-offset natural windows), pipeline-specific marking and sequence-order cues, scorer, and rubric. Stored and natural feature-score rankings were correlated (Spearman 0.732), and ranking harm was not shown.

fits_no_version.finding: Automated-interpretability explanation scores can be matched or beaten by explanation-free rules that read item construction. Examples: centre rule 0.979 against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers; sequence-order rule 0.227 against 0.160 for GPT-4. Score levels also change between stored and natural windows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated explanation scores for neurons and SAE features depend on evaluation-data construction (peak-centred crops, mark positions and counts, top-and-random sequence sets). Such scores are evidence about an explanation only when they beat explanation-free baselines.

record.code_released: Code and materials are stated to be released upon publication; URL not stated.
record.problems: No neuron polysemanticity classifications or prevalence estimates are measured. The stored fuzzing marks are rebuilt from inferred code; the large stored-run analysis is from one SAE, the Gemma comparison has 27 runs of 12 features, and the natural-window harm analysis uses one scorer and 49 features without a positive control on real data. The stored-versus-natural comparison also changes window length and composition. The matched-mark construction is derived but not tested. Jev’s API is not exactly deterministic.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional results about Jev and GPT-4 on 400 GPT-2 XL neurons, including rank correlations, within/between-sequence decompositions, causal-prefix checks, and open typed-decision-model comparisons. These were not included where they do not directly inform sensitivity of explanation scores to construction or scoring choice. Detection and fuzzing scorer comparisons in Appendix G were also omitted where they compare scorers on cued items without testing explanation quality.

untested.parts: No count of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models.
Causes without capacity pressure not tested.
No architecture or activation-function comparison of polysemanticity.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No neuron is classified as polysemantic under any scoring or activation-range choice. The study shows only that explanation scores depend on item construction.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V7 on the strength of the phrase 'how explanations are scored'. The study, however, never measures polysemanticity, so every link is removed and no verdict is given. Rows R10, R11, R14 and R17–R20 also concern the study's own scorer (Jev) or its own clean construction, not a measurement of the phenomenon.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether image-classifier neurons respond to unrelated visual inputs.
The study does not measure how many transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts.
The study does not test superposition or capacity pressure as a cause of polysemanticity.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
The study does not compare activation functions or architectures to measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence or performance costs.
The study does not investigate whether allegedly polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs.

The study tests how automated explanation scores vary with evaluation data and scoring choices, but does not test whether those changes alter a neuron’s classification as polysemantic or how often neurons receive that classification.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (500 random features)
rows.operation_detail: Measured balanced accuracy of an explanation-free rule on stored fuzzing items with marks rebuilt from inferred scorer code.

conditions.value: yes iff centre token is marked

rows.baseline: Stored LLM scorers: 0.838 (recomputed from stored per-item verdicts)
rows.note: The rule does not read the explanation. Mark positions are rebuilt from inferred code.
rows.check: Centre-rule balanced accuracy on rebuilt fuzzing marks is a benchmark shortcut. It says nothing about whether features are polysemantic.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B layer 20 Gemma Scope features
rows.operation_detail: Measured mark-only rules and stored scorer accuracy on rebuilt fuzzing marks.
rows.uncertainty: p = 1.0 × 10−5 for rule wins on 24 of 27 runs, loses on 2
rows.note: This is a benchmark-score shortcut result, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Count-rule shortcut on Gemma stored runs. No polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL neurons from OpenAI’s release
rows.operation_detail: Measured the sequence-mean oracle using each sequence’s true mean activation and nothing about tokens.
rows.note: This oracle uses true sequence means and is not an explanation-reading scorer.
rows.check: Sequence-mean oracle is a ceiling, not a rule. It measures score structure, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL neurons from OpenAI’s release
rows.operation_detail: Predicted activity on the first five listed sequences, without reading explanations.

conditions.value: predict 1 on first five sequences; post hoc

rows.uncertainty: p = 1.5 × 10−18 for rule scoring above GPT-4 on 287 of 400 neurons
rows.note: The paper says this shows what the data carry, not that GPT-4 used the ordering cue.
rows.check: Post hoc sequence-order rule. A benchmark shortcut only.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 natural-window features)
rows.operation_detail: Scored natural-text windows with Jev using the real feature explanations.
rows.uncertainty: 46 of 49 features; p = 7.0 × 10−11 against shuffled explanations
rows.note: The score is above the per-feature offset oracle (0.171) and sequence-mean oracle (η = 0.166), but is not a polysemanticity rate.
rows.check: Jev is the study's chosen scorer, so this row is the study's own method against a control. It does not measure polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 natural-window features)
rows.operation_detail: Scored the same natural-window examples with shuffled explanations.
rows.uncertainty: Jev with real explanations exceeded this on 46 of 49 features; p = 7.0 × 10−11
rows.note: Control showing that Jev’s natural-window score is not reproduced by shuffled explanations.
rows.check: Shuffled-explanation control for the study's own scorer.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 features with both data sets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared Jev’s simulation scores on stored snippets and natural windows.
rows.uncertainty: Scores were lower on natural windows for 44 of 49 features; p = 7.6 × 10−9
rows.note: The data sets also differ in length and composition, so this comparison does not isolate the position cue.
rows.check: Score-level difference between data sets. The comparison is confounded by window length and composition, and it is not a polysemanticity classification.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 features with both data sets)
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature rankings from Jev’s stored-snippet and natural-window scores.
rows.note: Stored scores tracked natural-window scores more closely than crop geometry (ρgeo = 0.512); the preregistered verdict was that ranking harm was not shown.
rows.check: Ranking stability of explanation scores, not of polysemantic labels.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 natural-window features)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the best fixed-position prior shared across features on natural windows.
rows.baseline: Preregistered bound: mean |r| ≤ 0.05 for centre and four-quarter priors
rows.note: A separate oracle choosing the best offset per feature using true activations scored 0.171.
rows.check: Position-prior check on the study's own clean windows. It validates the study's construction.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 features)
rows.operation_detail: Scored held-out token activations with a small encoder trained on stored snippets using explanations.
rows.baseline: Same architecture trained with no explanation: 0.438
rows.uncertainty: Two seed scores differed by less than 0.01
rows.note: The no-explanation model reached 83% of the full model’s held-out score.
rows.check: Trained-encoder shortcut check. Unrelated to polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small layer 8 residual-stream SAE (49 natural-window features)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the encoder trained on stored snippets on natural windows.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a drop on natural windows.
rows.check: A 'partial' state has no meaning against any version. This is a score drop for the trained encoder.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Automated explanation-score levels across evaluation-data constructions and scoring protocols
reader_labels.reason: Scores change across stored versus natural windows and rubric choices, while explanation-free construction rules can score highly on cued data (R1-R7, R12, R17-R20). These results support sensitivity of automated explanation scores to measurement choices, not changes in polysemantic-neuron classification.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature rankings across stored snippets and natural windows
reader_labels.reason: Although score levels differ, the stored-to-natural score ranking correlation is 0.732 and the study’s preregistered verdict was that ranking harm was not shown; the sample and comparison do not establish whether rankings change in general (R12-R13).
